opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that most agents today are built by taking a strong general-purpose model and wrapping it with prompts, tool descriptions, and some orchestration logic. That gets you surprisingly far, but it hits a ceiling. The model was never really trained to use *your* tools, in *your* environment, toward *your* objective. It's improvising based on what it picked up during pretraining and general instruction tuning.

Supervised fine-tuning is the obvious next step, but it has its own problems. You need demonstrations of good trajectories, and for multi-step tool use those are expensive to collect. More importantly, SFT teaches the model to imitate a path rather than to reach an outcome. When the agent goes slightly off-distribution, say a tool returns an unexpected error or a search comes back empty, an imitation-trained model often doesn't know how to recover, because it never saw that in the demonstrations.

RL changes the framing. Instead of saying "here's exactly what to do," you say "here's the environment, here are the tools, here's how we'll score the outcome, now figure it out." The model gets to explore, make mistakes, and learn from the consequences of its own actions. That's a much more natural fit for agentic behavior, which is inherently sequential and interactive. You saw this with reasoning models: once people started doing RL with verifiable rewards on math and code, you got emergent behaviors like backtracking and self-verification that nobody explicitly taught. I think the same thing can happen with tool use: learning when to call a tool, when not to, how to chain calls, how to recover from failures.

There's also a practical angle that excites me. With RL, you can often take a much smaller open model and train it on a specific task until it matches or beats a frontier model on that task, at a fraction of the cost and latency. For a lot of companies that's the difference between an agent that's a demo and one they can actually run in production.

And then the last piece is that the tooling has gotten good enough that this is no longer just something big labs can do. There are open frameworks now for rollouts, reward computation, and training loops in multi-turn environments. So part of what I'm pursuing is making that accessible: helping people define good environments and reward signals, because honestly that's where most of the hard work and most of the leverage is.

r001.rationale: The candidate says agents are built with prompts and orchestration and may hit a ceiling, but does not say developers may not understand why complex prompt sequences succeed or fail.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So the short version is that I think tool use is really the thing that separates a model that can talk about doing something from an agent that can actually do it. And when you look at how we've been building agents so far, most of it has been prompting. You take a frontier model, you write a really elaborate system prompt, you describe the tools, you give it a few examples, and you hope it figures out the orchestration on its own. And that works surprisingly well for demos. It works much less well when you put it in front of real users, real APIs, real failure modes.

The problem is that tool use is fundamentally a sequential decision problem. The model has to decide which tool to call, with what arguments, look at what comes back, decide whether that was good enough or whether it needs to try again, chain multiple calls together, recover from errors. That's not a single-shot prediction task. That's a trajectory. And supervised fine-tuning doesn't really capture that, because you're just imitating individual steps from some dataset, and the dataset usually doesn't contain the interesting cases, which are the ones where things go wrong partway through.

Reinforcement learning is the natural fit because you can define the reward at the level of the outcome. Did the agent actually complete the task? Did the API call succeed, did the code run, did the user get the answer they needed? And then you let the model explore and learn which sequences of tool calls get it there. You're optimizing the whole behavior rather than individual tokens.

The other thing I'd say, and this is partly from my time working on recommender systems at Google, is that I've seen what happens when you have a feedback loop and you actually train against it. The gains compound in ways that prompting just can't give you. With prompting you plateau pretty quickly. With RL, every bit of environment signal is something the model can learn from.

And honestly, what pushed us over the edge is that smaller models trained with RL on a specific set of tools can match or beat much larger general models on those tasks. That's a big deal for cost and latency when you're actually deploying agents. So that's the bet. Tool use is where agents live or die, and RL is the most direct way to get good at it.

r001.rationale: The response says developers write elaborate prompts and hope the model handles orchestration, but it does not say developers may not understand why those prompt sequences succeed or fail.

astra-6.text:
The reason is that tool use is really a sequential decision-making problem. An agent has to decide which tool to call, what arguments to give it, and then, based on what comes back, what to do next. You want to optimize that whole sequence for whether it actually accomplishes the task.

With supervised learning, you can show the model examples of successful sequences, and that’s a useful starting point. But there may be multiple ways to solve a problem, and the agent will encounter situations that aren’t covered by those examples. Reinforcement learning gives it a way to learn from the consequences of its choices: did this tool call help, did it get stuck, could it have reached the answer with fewer steps?

What’s appealing to me is moving from imitating a particular sequence of actions to learning how to achieve an outcome. The challenge, of course, is making sure the reward captures what you actually want the agent to accomplish.

r001.rationale: The response discusses agents choosing tool-call sequences and learning from outcomes, but does not say developers may fail to understand why complex prompt sequences succeed or fail.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is, an agent needs to do more than generate a good response. It needs to take actions—call a tool, look at the result, and decide what to do next. And those decisions have consequences over multiple steps.

With supervised learning, you can show the model examples of successful tool use. That gives you a useful starting point, but you’re teaching it to imitate a particular sequence. There may be several ways to solve the task, and when something unexpected happens, the model needs to recover rather than just follow the demonstrated path.

That’s why RL is interesting. You can let the model attempt a task and give it feedback based on whether it actually accomplished the goal. It can learn when a tool is useful, which tool to choose, what arguments to provide, and when it has enough information to stop. You can also account for things like the cost of unnecessary calls.

The hard part is getting the reward and the environment right. But tool use gives you opportunities to evaluate outcomes more concretely: did the action work, and did the agent complete the task? That makes it a compelling setting for learning from experience.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts supervised imitation with reinforcement learning and discusses tool outcomes, but it does not say developers may not understand why complex agent prompt sequences succeed or fail.
